subject: Science
stem: A torch bulb lights up only when the battery, wires, and switch together form a continuous, unbroken loop with no gaps. This continuous path through which electric current flows is called a:
explanation: Current flows only through a closed (complete) circuit — any break or gap (an open circuit) stops the flow and the bulb does not light.

subject: Science
stem: A metal wire allows electric current to pass through it easily, while the plastic covering around the wire does not allow current to pass at all. These two materials are respectively examples of:
explanation: Conductors (like metals) allow electric current to pass through easily; insulators (like plastic, rubber, wood) block current — this is why wires are covered with plastic/rubber insulation for safety.

subject: Science
stem: Several bulbs are connected one after another in a single loop (a series circuit). If one bulb's filament breaks, what happens to the other bulbs in the circuit?

options.option_text: All the other bulbs also stop glowing, since the circuit is broken at that one point
The other bulbs continue to glow normally
The other bulbs glow brighter than before
Only the bulb next to the broken one stops glowing

explanation: In a series circuit, there is only one path for current; a break anywhere in that single path stops current everywhere in the loop, so all bulbs go out — unlike a parallel circuit, where other branches keep working independently.

subject: Science
stem: When an insulated copper wire is wound around an iron nail and connected to a battery, the nail temporarily behaves like a magnet and can attract iron pins, but loses this property as soon as the battery is disconnected. This device is called a/an:
explanation: An electromagnet is a temporary magnet created by passing electric current through a coil wound around a soft iron core — its magnetism exists only while current flows, unlike a permanent bar magnet.
